title: Vietnam’s other trade deals could claim Washington’s wins
gist: Tran argues that most-favoured-nation clauses in Vietnam's 18 October EFTA agreement and the CPTPP could let Swiss, Norwegian, Australian, Japanese and Canadian firms claim any services or investment preferences Washington wins in its still-unpublished US–Vietnam trade deal, subject to reservations. Telecoms' 49% foreign-ownership cap is the clearest test case.

insights.claim: Vietnam says its trade agreement with the United States is 'essentially completed', but US officials are more cautious and no text has been published; the framework announced a year ago left digital trade, services and investment commitments to be finalised.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Text publication is the catalyst to watch for Vietnam services/investment market access.

insights.claim: A senior US Commerce Department official said the US trade deficit with Vietnam is its largest with any partner.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Vietnam remains a prime target for US trade pressure and concessions.

insights.claim: Whatever Washington secures in services and investment from Vietnam may not benefit American firms alone because Vietnam's other trade agreements could extend those gains to other partners.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Non-US firms (European, Australian, Japanese) could free-ride on US-won Vietnam market access.
insights.quote: Whatever Washington secures in services and investment, however, may not benefit American firms alone.

insights.claim: Vietnam signed an agreement on 18 October with EFTA (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein) whose Article 4.4 MFN clause requires 'immediately and unconditionally' no-less-favourable treatment for services suppliers versus any non-party, covering services measures generally.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: EFTA service providers could gain Vietnam access automatically matching US concessions.

insights.claim: The EFTA MFN clause exempts agreements meeting the WTO's comprehensive-services-agreement test and pre-listed measures; Vietnam's list names investment treaties, intra-ASEAN agreements, audiovisual co-productions and a maritime arrangement with Singapore.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Scope of carve-outs determines how much US access leaks to EFTA.

insights.claim: Washington's recent reciprocal agreements in the region do not appear to qualify as comprehensive services agreements, so EFTA governments could seek equal treatment or pursue state-to-state dispute settlement once the deal enters into force.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: US 'reciprocal' deal design weakens its ability to ring-fence preferences.
insights.locator: The clause does not hand EFTA

themes.theme: CPTPP route and telecoms test case

insights.claim: The CPTPP requires Vietnam to treat CPTPP investors and service suppliers, including from Australia, Japan and Canada, no less favourably than those of any other country, subject to reservations for pre-CPTPP agreements, ASEAN deals, later maritime, fisheries and aviation agreements, and sectoral carve-outs such as air transport and port operations.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: CPTPP members have a second legal route to US-equivalent Vietnam access.

insights.claim: Vietnam's CPTPP schedule records a 49% foreign-ownership ceiling for facilities-based basic telecoms, but its reservation on treating investors from different countries equally covers only rural/remote ethnic-minority networks, so if only US investors could exceed 49%, Australian, Japanese or Canadian investors could seek the same.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Telecoms is the sector to watch: a US carve-out on the 49% cap could open Vietnam telecom stakes to CPTPP investors.
insights.quote: a 49% foreign-ownership ceiling for facilities-based basic telecommunications services

insights.claim: Because the US and Vietnam have had a bilateral trade agreement since 2001, new concessions framed as amending it might fall within Vietnam's CPTPP reservation for earlier agreements, whereas the EFTA list has no comparable general reservation.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Legal framing of the US deal could be engineered to block CPTPP spillover; EFTA route is harder to avoid.

insights.claim: The MFN clauses will not be invoked often because many digital commitments, such as cross-border data transfer rules, are likely to apply to all partners anyway; they matter only where US firms get more favourable treatment.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Spillover is sector-specific, not across the board.

insights.claim: When the US–Vietnam text appears, Canberra, Tokyo, Bern and Oslo should check whether any treatment favours American firms in sectors Vietnam's other agreements cover, because some of Washington's gains may not stay American.
insights.speaker: Tran Hoang Tu Linh
insights.so_what: Expect allied governments to scrutinise the text for MFN claims.
